                                         PROJECT NO. 58000


    RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                             §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                         §               OF
    TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                    §             TEXAS
    THE ERCOT REGION



                     ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND’S COMMENTS ON
                      PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.192, §24.193, AND §25.252




Environmental Defense Fund (“EDF”) files the following comments in response to the
Commission’s proposal to adopt new 16 TAC 25.192, relating to Transmission Rates for Export
from ERCOT; and §25.193, relating to Distribution Service Provider Cost Recovery Factors
(“TCRF”); and new §25.252, relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs, as published in the Texas
Register on July 24, 2026 (“Proposal for Publication”). 1 The Commission requested comments be
filed by August 11, 2026, so these comments are timely filed.




1
    51 Tex. Reg. 4777 (July 24, 2026).

                                                 1
     I.      INTRODUCTION

         EDF appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s
(“Commission”) proposed amendments to 16 TAC §§ 25.192 and 25.193 and proposed new §
25.252 in Project No. 58000, Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost
Recovery in the ERCOT Region (“PFP”). 2

         The PFP implements key provisions of Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) and addresses how
transmission costs associated with large loads should be allocated and recovered within the
ERCOT region. Among other changes, the proposal establishes new requirements related to
transmission cost recovery for large load customers, including minimum billing demand
obligations and provisions governing the reservation of transmission capacity. These reforms come
at a critical time as Texas experiences unprecedented load growth, in large part due to interest from
data centers and other large computational loads. The Commission's decisions in this proceeding
will play an important role in determining whether this growth strengthens the electric system and
benefits consumers or results in increased costs and risks being shifted to existing ratepayers.

         EDF supports the Commission's efforts to ensure that the customers driving the need for
new transmission and distribution investments bear an appropriate share of the costs associated
with serving them. At the same time, the Commission should preserve incentives for large loads
to operate flexibly, efficiently utilize the capacity they reserve, and contribute positively to Texas's
electric grid. At this moment in time, Texas does hold an opportunity to attract economic
development and new electricity demand, but realizing the benefits of that growth will require
policies that align cost responsibility with cost causation, maintain affordability for existing
customers, and provide transparency regarding how reserved and utilized load affects transmission
planning and resource adequacy. Thus, EDF's general comments and suggested redlines focus on
ensuring that the Commission's implementation of SB6 protects ratepayers first and foremost,
while enabling a framework that encourages efficient grid utilization and supports long-term
reliability and affordability within ERCOT.




2
 Project No. 58000, Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT
Region, Staff Memo & Revised PFP w/August 11 Comment Deadline (July 2, 2026). [hereinafter “PFP”].

                                                    2
    1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
       different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different
       noncoincident (NCP) demands?
       EDF recommends the Commission establish different minimum demand values based on
the magnitude of the customer’s contracted peak demand. Large loads generally require more
substantial infrastructure investments, reserve greater amounts of system capacity, and can expose
existing customers to greater cost-shifting risk if projected load growth does not materialize.
Accordingly, it may be reasonable for the Commission to impose correspondingly stronger
minimum billing demand obligations on the largest customers.

       If the Commission elects to place greater weight on a particular metric for purposes of
differentiating among large load customers, EDF believes contracted peak demand provides the
stronger foundation. Contracted peak demand most directly reflects the level of service requested
by the customer and the transmission and distribution investments undertaken in reliance on that
request. Because planning and investment decisions must be made to serve the load that a customer
requests, rather than the load that is ultimately realized, contracted demand provides the clearest
link from a cost recovery standpoint.

       EDF recognizes that NCP demand may better reflect actual customer usage and, in some
circumstances, could support incentives for efficiency, load shifting, or other forms of flexibility.
Those considerations, however, are more appropriately addressed through mechanisms such as
phased adjustments, ratchets, or other refinements over time. At the outset, minimum billing
demand should reflect the capacity a customer has asked the system to reserve, while allowing the
Commission room to consider whether future adjustments are warranted once the utility has
recovered the costs incurred to serve that load.

       At the same time, EDF’s primary concern is not the specific percentages assigned to
particular customer classes, but rather ensuring that the overall framework fully recovers the
incremental costs incurred to serve large load customers, while also contributing a reasonable share
toward embedded system costs. This approach is necessary to protect existing ratepayers from
subsidizing the infrastructure investments required to serve new large loads. Any differentiation
should therefore be tied to the relative infrastructure investments, financial risks, and "but-for"
system impacts associated with serving larger loads, rather than arbitrary size thresholds. A well-
designed minimum billing demand framework can help achieve this objective, but it should not be

                                                   3
 viewed in isolation. Rather, it should operate as one component of the broader SB6 cost recovery
framework, alongside upfront interconnection fees, financial security requirements, contribution-
in-aid-of-construction payments, and other customer-funded protections contemplated in Project
No. 58481. 3 Together, these mechanisms can help ensure large load customers bear the costs they
cause, reduce the risk of stranded or underutilized investments, and protect existing ratepayers
from cost shifting.

         With respect to proposed rule language, EDF supports the Commission’s approach in §
25.193(d) of calculating minimum billing demand based on whichever is greater among a large
load customer’s contracted peak, non-coincident peak (“NCP”), or 12CP. 4 Each of these metrics
can capture different relevant operational and cost considerations, and using the highest of the
three can help ensure large load customers bear their fair share of the costs they impose on the
system. So long as the Commission’s chosen approach captures these considerations, remains
administratively practical, and does not introduce unnecessary complexity, EDF believes any of
these metrics, or a combination thereof, can serve as a reasonable basis for minimum billing
demand.

         EDF also recommends substantially clarifying or removing proposed § 25.193(d)(3). 5 As
drafted, the provision is difficult to interpret and reconcile. On the one hand, the requirement to
assess minimum billing demand "at the level of available service at the time it is available"
suggests that a customer's billing obligation should correspond to the amount of capacity that has
actually been made available by the utility at a given point in time. This language appears to
contemplate a form of phased and/or flexible energization, under which a customer receives
incremental access to capacity while transmission or distribution upgrades are completed. 6 On the
other hand, the phrase "irrespective of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully
using available capacity" could be interpreted to require billing based on the customer's full
contracted load, even before that full level of service has been made available. Because the




3
  See, e.g., upfront interconnection fees, financial security, and contribution-in-aid of construction payments. Project
No. 58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards (Jul. 31, 2025).
4
  PFP at 28.
5
  Id.
6
  Environmental Defense Fund, Let’s Get Flexible: Considerations for Unlocking Grid Capacity Using Flexible
Interconnection (Feb. 2025), available at https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/q812pd5afr3hboi61cm503fprla5ge0p.pdf

                                                           4
 provision can reasonably be read both ways, it is difficult to discern the Commission's intended
policy outcome.

       Accordingly, EDF recommends that, at minimum, the Commission revise the provision to
clearly specify how minimum billing demand applies when service is made available
incrementally and how billing obligations should change as additional capacity comes online. This
issue has significant implications for both cost recovery and customer incentives and is closely
intertwined with broader questions surrounding phased energization, flexible service
arrangements, and the efficient utilization of grid capacity. Given those broader policy
considerations, EDF believes these issues would be better addressed through a more
comprehensive framework specifically designed to govern phased and flexible interconnection
arrangements.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
             a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
             b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years;
             or c. extended to a longer time period?

       EDF declines to comment on this question at this time.


   3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
      lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
      load minimum billing demand:
             a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
             is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
             demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
             phases over the years, and how?
             b. be based on a “weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large
             load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
             customer' s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
             year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
             weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
             over the years, and how?

           As discussed above, EDF supports the Commission’s approach in § 25.193(d) of
   calculating minimum billing demand based on whichever is greater among a large load
   customer’s contracted peak, non-coincident peak (“NCP”), or 12CP.



                                               5
       4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
         entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
         Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
         electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
         cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
         legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
         loads.

           EDF declines to comment on this question at this time.



      5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
         transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve
         the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?
           EDF generally supports broadening the definition of transmission interconnection costs to
include transmission projects identified through a batch study when those projects are necessary
to accommodate the transmission needs of a particular group of large loads. 7 Transmission
investments are often driven by the cumulative impact of multiple large load requests rather than
a single customer in isolation. Where a batch study identifies network upgrades that are needed to
serve the transmission capacity requirements of a defined set of large load customers, cost
allocation should reflect that shared causation rather than treating each project as though it were
unrelated to the broader transmission need.

           Broadening the definition in this manner would better align cost responsibility with the
customers whose interconnection requests drive the need for new transmission infrastructure while
reducing the likelihood that those costs are shifted to existing ratepayers. It would also recognize
the practical reality of modern transmission planning, where utilities and system operators
increasingly evaluate clusters of large load requests together to identify the most efficient network
solutions. Limiting transmission interconnection costs to projects directly attributable to a single
load could understate the infrastructure investments required to serve a group of customers that
collectively create the need for transmission upgrades. Accordingly, when a batch study
demonstrates that specific transmission projects are necessary to accommodate the transmission
capacity needs of a particular set of large loads, those costs should generally be treated as
transmission interconnection costs associated with those customers. To clarify this, EDF

7
    PFP at 12.

                                                   6
 recommends the revisions in bold below to the definition of “Transmission Interconnection Costs”
in § 25.192(b).

                                           § 25.192(b)

(13) Transmission interconnection costs -- All costs associated with the facilities required to
physically interconnect, or upgrade the interconnection of, a transmission-level customer or a
distinct group of transmission-level customers to the existing transmission system, or a distinct
set of transmission-level customers, to the existing transmission network, including
interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary
to establish or modify service. Transmission interconnection costs include, but are not limited
to, interconnection facilities, interconnection lines, transmission substation additions or
modifications, transmission upgrades, network upgrades, and any associated equipment or
facilities necessary to establish, maintain, or modify service. The term also includes
transmission projects identified through an interconnection, cluster, or batch-study process that
are demonstrated to be necessary to accommodate the transmission capacity needs of a specific
customer or distinct group of customers and that would not have been required absent the
customer's or customers' interconnection request.

   6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
      the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
      these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
      transmission planning studies?
       EDF believes resource adequacy reports, assessments, and transmission planning studies
should reflect both reserved transmission capacity and actual operational demand. If a large load
customer reserves significant transmission capacity, that reservation drives planning decisions and
may necessitate transmission investments regardless of whether the customer has fully energized
or is utilizing the capacity today. Excluding reserved capacity from planning assessments could
therefore understate future system needs. At the same time, relying solely on reserved capacity
could overstate near-term demand if load materializes more slowly than expected.

       Accordingly, the Commission should require ERCOT and transmission providers to track
and report both metrics. Resource adequacy reports and planning studies should distinguish
between contracted capacity and realized demand, providing greater transparency into how much
reserved capacity is being utilized and how much remains idle. In addition, reporting on unused
                                                7
 reserved capacity could help planners and policymakers better understand the potential flexibility
value of these loads and identify opportunities to improve grid utilization. Where customers have
reserved capacity but are not fully utilizing it, that information may provide insight into available
system flexibility and help inform future planning, forecasting, and infrastructure investment
decisions.

       For this section, the Commission may want to consider adding a new section to the rule
section § 25.192(f)(1), which already governs ERCOT's determination of billing demand and
treatment of large loads:

                                               § 25.192(f)(1)

       (C) ERCOT shall track for each large load customer subject to §25.194 of this title
       (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards), both:

               (i) the transmission capacity reserved or contracted by the customer; and

               (ii) the customer's realized demand, including its non-coincident peak demand
               and 12CP demand.
               Such tracking shall capture the amount of reserved capacity that is not being
               utilized and shall be incorporated into resource adequacy reports, resource
               adequacy assessments, and transmission planning studies to support evaluation
               of future system needs, utilization of existing infrastructure, and potential load
               flexibility.

    II.      CONCLUSION

         EDF thanks the Commission for the opportunity to provide these comments.

Dated: August 11, 2026
